reference.source: Fraser and Paré's Diagnosis of Diseases of the Chest
clinicalPearls: Characterised by focal obliteration or interruption of the lumen of a segmental or subsegmental bronchus, with normal development of the airways and alveoli distal to the atretic segment.
The apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe is the classic site, although any lobe may be affected.
Mucus secreted distal to the blind-ending bronchus cannot drain and accumulates as a mucocoele (bronchocoele), producing the characteristic branching tubular gloved-finger opacity.
The lung distal to the lesion is ventilated only through collateral channels (pores of Kohn, canals of Lambert), causing regional air trapping and hyperinflation.
Most cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging in adolescents or young adults.
CT is diagnostic, showing the combination of a mucocoele with surrounding oligaemic, hyperlucent, hyperinflated lung.
It must be distinguished from an obstructing endobronchial tumour or foreign body, which are acquired causes of a similar appearance.
Management is usually conservative, with segmentectomy or lobectomy reserved for recurrent infection or diagnostic uncertainty.
reference.pathophysiology: Bronchial atresia is thought to result from a focal interruption of the developing bronchus, attributed either to an in-utero vascular insult to the bronchial supply or to a defect in bronchial budding occurring after the distal airway has already formed. The consequence is a segmental bronchus that ends blindly, with normal lung parenchyma beyond it. Secretions produced by the mucosa distal to the atresia have no route of egress and collect to form a mucus-filled bronchocoele, while the distal parenchyma, receiving air only via collateral ventilation and unable to expel it efficiently, becomes hyperinflated and oligaemic through reflex hypoxic vasoconstriction.
additionalDifferentials: Endobronchial tumour such as carcinoid causing mucoid impaction
Inhaled foreign body with distal air trapping
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis with mucoid impaction
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution and contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax
Bronchoscopy to exclude an obstructing endobronchial lesion
Contrast-enhanced MRI to characterise mucocoele signal
Ventilation-perfusion assessment showing a matched regional reduction
Pulmonary function testing if disease is extensive
Histopathological examination of any resected specimen
redFlags: A new or enlarging soft-tissue component suggesting tumour rather than a benign mucocoele
Recurrent infection localised to the affected segment
Haemoptysis, which should prompt exclusion of malignancy
Progressive hyperinflation causing mediastinal shift or respiratory compromise in a neonate
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent; most patients remain asymptomatic for life, and those requiring resection for complications generally do very well.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the mucocoele as a neoplasm and proceeding to unnecessary aggressive intervention.
Conversely, assuming a mucoid-impaction pattern is congenital and missing an obstructing endobronchial cancer in an older patient.
Overlooking the surrounding hyperlucency, which is the key clue distinguishing it from other tubular opacities.
Confusing the entity with pulmonary sequestration when imaging is incomplete.
references: Fraser and Paré's Diagnosis of Diseases of the Chest
management: Observe asymptomatic incidental lesions, which is appropriate for most patients
Exclude an obstructing endobronchial tumour or foreign body mimicking the appearance using CT and bronchoscopy
Treat any superimposed distal infection with appropriate antibiotics
Offer surgical resection by segmentectomy or lobectomy for recurrent infection, significant symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty
Arrange interval imaging follow-up for conservatively managed lesions
Refer to respiratory medicine and thoracic surgery for assessment
